blocks.x: Okay, let me see, I'll check the microphone just to get a little something on here. Today is January the 4th, is that right? Correct. January 4th, 1962, and we're recording at 1515 North Roman Street. Can we get your name on here? Full name? Ah, Boy Bang Senior. And your name? Book Free World. And I'm Dick Allen. Good, I think I got it going. I think we got most of your life down before, but I just want to follow up on some of the things. How is your brother tied in with these picnics? I don't really quite understand that. One of them days, there was a lot of people who had picnics. It just was a pleasure to him, you know. He'd just get picnics and he'd hire family. He'd have tickets. It wasn't that he'd make no profit on it. He just loved that. Would he do it every day on the weekends? No, he'd do that maybe about, oh I guess about two, three times during the summer. And what day of the week would it be? Oh it would mostly be on Sunday. And where were they held? They were held at Mellon Boyd. Any particular pavilion? Well they had a lot of camps along there. I forgot the name of some of them, but they had Lucian Pavilion.
We had so many. I just can't say the name of them. No. How would they look?

How would the different camps look? Well most of them look about the same. Just like a large room with a top on it. What way would they be different from say Mamalu's? Because I've been to Mamalu's. You've been to Mamalu's? Well not much. Not much. It's about the same as those Little Woods camps. Yeah. Citrus, that area. Yeah.

Well they have the band inside the building. Yeah. And they would dance inside the building too? Yeah. No platformer or nothing for a band. They just sit on them, blow in them. Pick a coin and sit and go. Well the rooms must have been fairly large then. The what? The rooms must have been fairly large. Yeah.

And straight chairs I guess or something like that. What kind of chairs? Straight chairs. It's on there straight chairs and the people would be sitting around there. Would they have the chairs in the middle of the floor? No, no chairs for the people. They would have to have to have to have to have to have to have to have them. Oh I see. People would have to sit down. They would stand and walk and dance. Do they have food at these affairs? Have what? Food for them? Oh yeah. Food and chairs. Well beer, you know, no whiskey. Soft drinks and billiards they have. There you go. Tell me about the food. I'd like to hear about that. Well they take and they make maybe a couple of dish pans of potato salad and buy a ham or two and boil them and prepare them, you know. And they fix up the food at home and take it out there and all they have to do is just make the sandwiches or the plates whatever it is. To be a problem. Yeah. They just use those paper plates.
What did they have, like a long table with the food on it?

Well they had a table they'd use. They'd put up a table sometime. But most of the time you just get your food, you know, go off and eat it. They'd had seats around the side, all around the side. You know, something like that. I don't know if you've ever been in. You have never been in the frozen leahaw. Anyway, that's where some of the halls had seats, you know, all around the wall. Just like a bench. Yeah, like all that jobs I mean I said to.
Do it? No, I don't think so. No, something like that.

They had some benches around the wall. They did? No. I don't know. I don't know. I don't see them. They must have been sitting on my imagination. It seems to me we were sitting on chairs. Yeah, but around the wall I think they had some benches somewhere. I don't know.
Maybe they did. Maybe they did.

Do you remember many of the… Well, I know another one I want to ask you. How did they serve the beer? Would it be in bottles or what? Oh no, keg beer. Keg beer? Yeah, that's all they used to use that time. Things like that. Would the people fish? Very… No. Just good time and pleasure, huh? Just come out there and have a little fun dancing and so forth. How long would it last? What would it last? What would it last? It would last… The band would come out there. I don't exactly remember but the band would come out there around about eleven o'clock. And they would play until about five or six o'clock at the evening. But not at nine. No. What bands would they have out there now? Oh yeah. Used to have Mount Everest… I've forgotten the name of the bands because I was small at them time. Well just some of the people. I just remember some of the people. And Mount Everest… And Mount Everest… And… I remember a big guy I know of… And Mount Everest… And Mount Everest… How many pieces would the bands have? Only one of the bands… And Mount Everest… How many pieces would the bands have?
How many pieces would the bands have? Only six… It wouldn't be but six…

About six. That's all they used to do. I guess they used a banjo, huh? Used to use a banjo. They never used no piano in an old Dixie Ladd band. You're never singing that. What about you? Always a banjo. Guitar ever? Would they ever have a guitar player? Ghetto? Not that I remember. Let me check a little of this. See, I was wondering about some of the clarinet players that you admired out there. Well, I admired Big I, Lou, and Lorenzo Tio. I used to admire Pico, too. Well, do you think you'd play anything like those fellas that you admired at that time? I don't know. I couldn't answer that. Do you think anybody influence your style that you play today? A lot of people tell me that George Lewis and I play as pretty much alike. I don't know. I think that is about the closest one. Some of your licks are the same I've noticed, you know. But did you ever hear George in those days? When you were all? No. Well, you heard the same people, so it figures your ideas should be alike, you know. I mean, without ever thinking about it, if you listen to the same people, the ideas are going to be the same. Did you ever try to copy anybody's style in particular? No. What about listening to records? Did you ever listen to records in those times when you were young? I used to listen to records before I started playing, before I started playing.
Who were some of the people that you liked to listen to on records?
I used to like the Bruce singers, I used to like, I used to like Bruce singers like Ava Walsh, Mamie Smith.
Did you like the Karnath players on those records? Oh yeah. Jim Noon.
I haven't heard much of Jim Noon, but Johnny Dodds. You liked this playing, huh? I admired this style.

Well, getting back to the bands at these picnics, there would be six pieces. Yeah, that's right. And there'd be a clarinet, and what else? A clarinet, a tromborong, a trumpet, a bass, a drum, and a band. I understand you. Do they play anything like that? Do they play Dixieland now, would you say?
No. Pretty much. Slower or faster? Well, slower than what we play.
You mean at the paddock? Yeah. At the paddock.
Yeah, yeah.
Did they take a lot of solos like at the paddock? No. No.

They took a lot of solos. So there were some differences in them. Yeah, sure. The band just played along. Nobody stood up and took solos. A man might put a take down. A fella take down and he'd have to play a couple of chords and the band just keep on. When he come back up somebody else, take down. That's how they used to play in them games. What about the banjo? Would he ever take a solo? No. Well, not that. No, I don't think. If so, I don't remember. Drum solos then? No. And bass? I don't remember bass or any of those. I was forgetting to be taking solos in them days. Yeah.

So what would happen if one of the horns got tired, he'd take down, then the other two would play? Yeah, let's keep going. The other two would play? Yeah. Would there ever be a time when there was just one horn playing? Like just a trumpet or just a clarinet? Well, I guess so, yeah.
What would he play? Would he play a lead or variations or what? Just the one horn going? Well, that I don't remember. I don't remember.
Would the people applaud for solos like they do at the paddock now, you know, when somebody stands up and takes a solo, and the next fellow stands up and takes a solo?

No, it was just when the dance, when the number was over, people would just stop dancing and say, I don't tell you, play another number. It's pretty hard to applaud. Why are you dancing? It would be about five minutes. The band would rest between the numbers about five minutes. They'd take a blow and then play another number. It was nothing like they do now. Well, you don't ever get tired at the paddock, do you? Oh, I get tired sometimes. Well, how long do you have between numbers there? Well, between numbers there, it seems to me you don't have any time. It seems to me too. Yeah. What's the slowest tempo you ever played at? I mean, during the course of an average night, do you play many slow numbers there? No. What about at a dance? Would you play many slow numbers? Well, at a dance it all depends who you play for. You have to feel the people out and see what they like the best. How do you tell what they like the best? Well, by playing a slow number. Paying attention. I mean, they get on the floor. They play no medium. They play no fast one. Whatever one you see they take to the best, you know, that's what they want. That's what they like the best. So your idea then is to please the public on a dance, right? I think that's the best idea too. I better please the public on a dance. Well, I don't think that always happens on Bourbon Street myself. I don't think they're playing the police the public there a lot of times. Oh, no. I don't think that. They're playing the police the night club on. I don't want to make you say that, but that's what I think.

You know? That's something else. Well, then the bands that you first started playing yourself, did they play like these old picnic bands, or more like the band at the paddock now? No, more so like the picnics bands you should play. In other words, you wouldn't take a lot of solos or anything? No. Would you have any numbers where you featured a special part, a special kind of solo, like on High Society, say? Like that time that was about the home and when they're out and during that?
Yeah.
Yeah.

Well, now, when you play High Society, I know you play that part that everybody plays, and then you go home and play another variation. Where did you get that second variation from? Well, it's just my own idea. I just make anything up to my mind. Mm-hmm. Well, that's a very nice solo. I've always liked that through the years.

I think that's a good one. There's another number. I know there's a special kind of featured Kranath part. That's St. Louis Blues. I know you and Piku, Rie Lee Barnes, George Lewis, all play that one special little part, you know, that chorus. That you mean that solo? Yeah.

Well, that's a, that solo, that's been, that was on orchestration. That's the first, that's the first solo I learned to play in St. Louis Blues. Of course, I makes it a little different from because it was, you know, I could brush it up a little, but most of it is just, it was, that was written. It was written. Do you remember the first time you saw it? It was an orchestration, and all of, all of the time they played, they made that. That's when you go real high. Yeah. Well, you read it off the orchestration yourself? Yeah. You can read then, huh? I don't call myself a reader, I call myself a scholar. That's how I worked, it offered orchestration. Uh-huh. Do you remember how I worked orchestration? No, but then I would, you know, make a little difference, put something, I think, a little something in it that I think sounded better. When did you start playing, what year was that you started playing professionally? You know, your first job. My first job? See, I'd say around about 19, what 19, 20. Not long after the war then, huh? No. No, not long after the war. What band was it you played your first job with? My first job was with, uh, Isabel Morgan. That's your first band job, not just two places. Yeah, first band job. That was for Isabel Morgan at the Ortiz in the hall. Mm-hmm. And, uh, who was in the band? Do you remember those guys? No, I just can't remember. Yeah, I was a little bit of the same band. Isabel Morgan. Yeah, I was a leader. Yeah. Let's see. That's funny, you wouldn't have Andrew there. Was Andrew playing there? Or was he there too? No, uh, I'm going to miss me. That's okay. I'm a little missy. What? That wasn't, uh, I was wrong, that was Ormer Bernard. Your first band job was Ormer Bernard. Yeah, my first job was Ormer Bernard at the Ortiz in the hall. Mm-hmm. See, because Adolf Alexander used to play with him. Them bids and fosters would get a better job, job pay more, they'd just send somebody else, they'd get anybody sent in the place. And Adolf Alexander once sent me in his place. Mm-hmm. Did you make that well? Well, best I could. Did you play many numbers there? Yeah, but, uh, I didn't play but the lead almost, so.
Well, he didn't play but the melody. You weren't making many variations then? No. But when did you start to do that? Well, I guess we practiced.

Just used to practice hard, you know. Every time I hear somebody make a vary, I'd whistle it until I get home, grab my horn, feel for it on my horn. Did you have a play along? I didn't think it would sound good to me. I did. Mm-hmm. Did you ever play along with anybody else, with records or with a piano, or any of those times, to study? Well, I used to play with my brother a lot. I was standing together, and he played a little piano. Mm-hmm. I ain't surprised it was him. Yeah. Yeah.

Yeah. Was there any special clarinet players that you used to hear and get ideas from? You know, things that you'd whistle and then play there? Well, I think I like a little bit from the Sender County guys. Yeah. On the records? Yeah.
I'm back to your brother. Did he play with bands ever? No. He had started out on drums. He just played a few jobs. He'd keep them all. What was his name? Paul. Paul Garland.
Your dad, did he play any music, your father? No.
When I was a boy, I know my dad had a bandolet, but I don't know if I ever remember him playing.
Did you say he was a carpenter? Did somebody say that? A painter. A painter.
Did any of your uncles play or grandfather? I don't know. I just took it up because I just liked clarinet so much. A band without a clarinet.
There was no band with me. Do you still feel like that? Yeah.

Do you have a play saxophone? No. Would you play one if somebody gave you one? I don't know because it might throw me back on that outer system clarinet. That's why I never bought everybody. You never even owned a saxophone? Well, I bought one. I bought a soprano.
I got a soprano from the store and kept it two leasing and gave it back. Well, that's pretty much like Mealy Barnes. He won't play one. And I think George gave his away there, huh?

I think so. He don't like it. He had one. Just not necessary. It's too much difference. He was in the band. He was in the band. He was in the band. Who was with Omar Bernard's band? Buddy Bernard, he was on the band, Joe. I believe Rodgers, who died. He used to live on the main street. It's a drummer? Yeah. Ernest Rodgers? Ernest Rodgers. He was on the drum. And ever heard of Ambrose, the drum roll? Yeah. Yeah. Thomas Tophie's uncle. That's right. He was on drum roll. Bass. From that age, I think he was on bass. It might have been Thomas Copeland. Well, who was this guy called? O-T. O-T. O-T. O-T. O-T. That's who was playing bass. O-T. Well, who was he though? What was his name? That's all I know about. I see. You know if that was a nickname, or his first name, or his last name? I don't know. I always thought it was a nickname.
You said that was a dance album? It was a dance? Yeah, it was a dance. What, did they sell tickets? Yeah.
Was that by, by Flava? Do you remember one name? No, I don't remember.
So on that job, you mostly just played the melody, huh?

Yeah, on that job. That was, that was true. Our time with Margie, it just came out. Uh-huh. Yeah. Now that on a date, we couldn't find out when Margie came. Huh? We can tell the date because we couldn't find out when Margie came. Yeah. Did you, you didn't remember who was an Isaiah Morgan's band? No. His brothers were born in that time? No. No. No. Kim used to be with him sometime. Uh-huh. And uh, Andrew too. Uh-huh.
Did you begin to work with this band on a regular basis? Who was that on the band on? Yeah.

Well, after, when the fellows would see me coming on a job, a guy would send me pretty often, you know? And when they'd see me coming on a job, I could see that they wasn't satisfied. Uh-huh. But he sent me so often and I would practice so hard, you know, to do better every time I'd go. So, oh my. Bernard asked me one night, he said, look, you want to belong to my band? Yeah. I said, well, sorry, me if the fellows are satisfied. I said, uh, you know, you got this other band. He said, that's all right. If you can play one night, you can play all the time. He said, now you want to belong to him? I said, well, sure. So, I'll start waiting with him. After I go for the exam, he had money begun. Bigaud used to do the same thing, see? He said to me every time he'd get another job. So, it was Bonnie Bigaud playing with him at the time that he took me right off. What happened to Bonnie? Well, he just got tired of him laying off. I thought maybe he left town or something. No, I just got tired of him laying off.
Was he playing clarinet then or saxophone? He said clarinet. When did he take up saxophone, do you know? No, I don't. Well, what was the next band after that that you played with?

I played with the Olinca band. He had an eight-piece band. As I know, the pass on drum and the album of Tablet, trumpet. He had a Henry Julian on saxophone. Is that a sax and clarinet? Yeah. It used, yeah, we used two trumpets, sax and clarinet, made of eight pieces. No trombone? Yeah, one trombone, bass and a banjo. What would he have on saxophone? Sometimes it would be Hoybert Moran, different fellas. For a while he had whatever it was Moran.
So many of them. Yeah. Did they play from sheet music? It's a big band. Well, yeah.

At that time, that was the goal, you know, to make these bands and playing the orchestration. So I played with them a good while until I got a regular job on the canal in London. It was the Alamo we had there. I got a job there with Willie Paiso. Where did they play there? What kind of music? Jitney. Feet music? Or was it a hand cell? No, no. No, just didn't have time to fool with no music because you pick up number one behind the other, nothing but chorus. And people get there and dance. A man come in the place and buy a lot of tickets. That's a piece. You cut the numbers off short. Each dance was a ticket. They'd tear a ticket off from his role. Would you play one chorus or two chorus? I played two or three. Sometimes I played just two. Sometimes I played maybe four or five.
I played a lot. I'll give my break, huh? Mm-hmm. Well, did you enjoy playing from the arrangements more or playing just head arrangements?

No, I enjoy playing the head and bolts. Because playing those and rake and a lot of the things, it seems to me it didn't sound half as good as what I could make myself. Mm-hmm. I wanted to ask you about Walter LaVernie. Did he play with any bands? Well, he used to play, but I don't know with who. I don't think he was with any regular band. I think the fellas used to hire him now and then. Yeah. But he taught you, huh? He started me off. He knew something about music. Yeah, he knew them. Did he teach you anything about breathing? I often wondered about your system of breathing. No, he taught me to the way I lift the horn. He learned me that. I remember Russell talked about that when he taught you before. How do you breathe? What sort of system do you use? You play very long phrases sometimes, I just wonder. Yeah, well, I just can't explain that. You don't even think about it? No, I just don't think about it. Mm-hmm. I guess a lot of guys do things right and don't even know what they're doing right. That's right. Just comes natural, huh? Just comes natural. But none of your teachers instructed you on that? No.
That's a funny thing. Did this world of the Verney play kind of anything like you play it now?

Well, I'll tell you the truth. I never did. I ain't never even hoid him to play with a man. Mm-hmm. I never hoid him to play. I couldn't tell you that. Where were you brought up anyway? Here in the city. Well, we'll start the beginning. Where were you falling exactly? I was falling right down here in the Sempern Hall. Ellen and Priya. Ellen and Priya? It's not far from him. And where have you lived? Did you say that most of your life? No. Well, I don't remember that address. But the next place that I remember was 2021 Allen Street. That was Galveston. And Johnson. And how were you when you moved to that address? Well, that's the... That's the... That's the... That's the place that I remember.

Reel 2, Albert Burbank, January the 4th, 1962. You say you will work with many bands, huh? Yeah. Such as? Such as Buddy P.T., Kid Thomas. When did you work with Thomas? Well, that's way back, but I just can't remember. Before the break and after? Why do you remember? I don't remember if it was before or after. But I worked with him for a pretty good while, I guess for about a year or so. He did. I didn't know that. He's waiting across the room. He had a job on weekends. I played with Buddy P.T. for a good while. While our jobs was mostly out of town, he used to go to Buckaloozie and go through Mississippi, just get jobs out of those places. A lot of times in Buckaloozie, he would give the dance. He would give the dance on a 60-40 basis. I don't know what else I'd take him. He would split the band. How much would Buddy get, 60 or 40? The band would get 40. What would Buddy get? He didn't get 35 and he got five. He would get 40.
Well, who's selling tickets then? Is Buddy selling tickets himself?
He has somebody. He always has somebody that he knows or somebody out of the band.
Would he sell them before the dance started or would he just wait until the same day?

Yeah. How many trumpet players does Buddy have in his band? Himself. No other? No other. It's a six piece band. Is anybody around that plays anything like Buddy? Sometimes he can count himself. Anybody around that plays anything like Buddy? No.
I don't know anybody that plays anything like Buddy. What kind of a style did he have? Was he loud?

He wasn't so loud and he wasn't a high note man. He made so much in the race and stuff. Would he play lead all the time? No. He'd get all. He'd get all. Would you ever carry the lead with him very long? He'd make a lot of chords. Would he play back to you when you had the lead or not? Sometime. What kind of a part would he play there? Would he play some? He'd make a second. Make a second to you. Second drumming part.
You would play the melody, he'd make a second.

Who else was in that band? I see. Samuel Penn was playing drum. George Washington was playing drum. I don't remember. I just can't remember the other voice. What about Sammy Penn in those days? Did he play as loud as he does now? Yeah. He's plenty loud now. Did he make a lot of explosions and stuff then or was he more of a straight drum or what? He's played very much like he's playing now. But I think he's more improved now. I see.
You like to work with him? Oh yeah.

I wanted to ask you something. How many bands would you be playing with at one time? Say you're playing with one guy, Kid Thomas for example, on the weekends. How many other bands would you be working with during the course of the week? Well, like I know, I'm waiting with Kid Thomas. Weekends would be maybe Friday, Saturday, Sunday. Just anything come along in between that with anybody else, I'd just take it. That would be sometimes two or three nights, you know. You might be working with four bands at once, huh? Sure.
Did you have a day job at this time during these years? Oh yeah. Always, yeah. Always kept a day job. What kind of a day job?
I was, I used to work in a shoe factory. Were you a shoe maker? No. I was a stock cutter in a shoe factory.

And then you'd just play music in the evening? Yeah. Would you take a job at night, say you had to go to your shoe factory job in the daytime? Could you play a music job at night? Oh yeah. I could take it in them beds.

It's a little late now. I want to ask you something. Do you think playing music is worth it? Or not? Well, it's worth it to me. I mean, it seems like you had to study hard and work hard on it. It was worth it back then, huh? Yeah. Just getting a wire guy to play his music. It's worth it. I think it's worth it to the ones that can make a living off of it. Can do good at it. There's so many, there's so many that, that, uh, learned it and, before all their time said, they just don't get a break. Places do it now, they have to go on some other kind of work.
Would you rather just play music or do something else? No, I'd rather just play music. Why?

Well, because I love it. And I enjoy it. But I wouldn't enjoy doing any other kind of work. What about in those times when you'd work with Oma and Ramon and bands like that, would you make any money to market anything? Well, it didn't appear like now. All you'd make was, uh, at them time, the prices was, uh, I think about just about a dollar an hour. You'd pay a five-hour charge, you'd make five hours. Well, with that five hours, could you buy as much then as you buy with your day's salary at the paddock now? Uh, I imagine, I'd say, I imagine so. So you were, you were getting just as much in terms of what you could buy with it. That's right. Things were so much cheaper in the days.
But most of the fellas still have day jobs, most of the musicians kept other jobs too. Is that right?

Well, there were some of them that had day jobs. A lot of them didn't do anything to play music because at that time you had so much work. You didn't have those jukeboxes and things that's cutting you out of weight.
Was there ever a time when you didn't have a day job back in the twenties and thirties? Yeah.
You could just make enough by playing music because, uh, yeah, I made, I, after the jukeboxes and throw it down, when I was out of weight for a while, I just was making all the music.
Did you ever play with Danny Barker back then? Yeah. Yeah.

I believe, if I'm not mistaken, I believe Danny Barker played about his first job with me. Uh huh. Out in high, I had a three piece job out at the lake on Lake Front there. We was working on a thing every night. And I got Danny Barker in a drum. We got that for, oh, I guess about a year or a better.
Was that every night of the week or just weekends? That was every night. Every night? Yeah.
What did Danny play then? Banjo.

Banjo, that's before he switched to guitar. It must have been hard on you. You had to carry a lot of melody. Oh yeah. I had to stay up too. Uh huh. Couldn't take down much. Would you get tired? Sometimes.
Would you get as tired as you get as a pad now? No. No. Even though you were the only one? I guess you played numbers in slower tempos. Yeah. Did they have a lot of that around?

Little groups with just a clarinet and no trumpet? Yeah, they had a lot of that because they were just a clarinet and no trumpet. Yeah, they had a lot of that because they were just a clarinet and no trumpet. Yeah, they had a lot of that because you take a lot of the more rooms. You still have little three people in the middle of the middle of the middle of the

Did you ever go into the tunks and play there? No. Did you ever hear any clarinet plays in the tunks? The real rarity guys? I don't remember, no. In fact, you said tunk. Now what do you mean by tunk? I mean a real low-round place where they would just maybe have a piano, a little three-piece band. I mean the Red Onion, the Vulkas. No, I never used to go around in complex.
Did you ever hear of clarinet plays in town that could play real good blues? What? Blues.
Did I ever hear? Yeah, outstanding blues players here. Did you ever specialize in all the blues? Yeah. No, not that often. No. Did Big Island, we played a lot of blues? No. How about Piku?
Yeah. See, them bands in them days, Trump, they was a leader and whatever he played, just

baller. Did you ever change your style much when you played with different bands? another trumpet player that would play one way with one band. another trumpet player that played a different way? They played pretty much the same with Buddy Petit as with Kid Thomas. Yeah. They played pretty much the same with Buddy Petit as with Kid Thomas. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah.

There was a Trump McLeod from Slidell. He used to play with a lot too. He used to work through Mississippi and he used to send for Samuel Penn and I. Thomas Parker, you ever heard of? Leonard Parker. Leonard Parker. You ever heard of Leonard Parker? Sure, George Lewis used to play with him. I know he's better too. And I knew Dan Moody. Dan Moody used to be in a band too.

segments.title: Session opening; brother's picnics and the camps where they were held
segments.summary: Allen opens the tape (Jan 4, 1962). Burbank explains his brother's summer picnics at lakefront camps, the halls, and bands playing on the floor.

segments.title: Food, beer and hours at the picnics
segments.summary: Describes the potato salad and ham, paper plates, keg beer, benches or chairs, and the band playing from about eleven till evening.

segments.title: Picnic band lineup, clarinetists and records that shaped him
segments.summary: Picnic bands ran about six pieces with banjo and no piano. He admired Lorenzo Tio and Pico; people say he plays like George Lewis.

segments.title: Picnic-band style compared with the band at the Paddock; solos and tempos
segments.summary: Old picnic bands played slower, with little soloing, rested five minutes between numbers, and played to please the dancers, unlike today's club work.

segments.title: High Society and his own variations
segments.summary: Burbank says his High Society variation is his own idea.

segments.title: St. Louis Blues solo from orchestration and his first band job with Bernard
segments.summary: He learned the St. Louis Blues solo from an orchestration, then recalls his first job, substituting for Adolf Alexander in Ormer Bernard's band, and practicing to learn variations.

segments.title: Brother Paul, his father and relatives who played music
segments.summary: He played with his brother, who had a little piano and drums; his father painted and owned a mandolin but no one else played.

segments.title: Why the clarinet and his attitude to saxophone
segments.summary: He took up clarinet because he loved it; he owned a soprano sax briefly and others like Barnes and George Lewis dislike saxophone.

segments.title: Personnel of Ormer Bernard's band
segments.summary: Names the drummer, bass player O-T and others in Bernard's band, and the dance with tickets; he mostly played melody.

segments.title: Becoming a regular in Bernard's band
segments.summary: Bernard saw him being sent as a sub, offered him a place, and he replaced Bonnie Bigaud who kept laying off.

segments.title: The eight-piece Olinca band
segments.summary: Describes the eight-piece band with two trumpets, sax, clarinet, trombone, bass, banjo and drums that read orchestrations.

segments.title: Dance-hall job on Canal Street with Willie Paiso
segments.summary: At the Alamo he played ticket dances with Paiso, choruses cut short, two to five choruses per number.

segments.title: Head arrangements versus written parts; teacher Walter LaVernie and breathing
segments.summary: He prefers playing by head; LaVernie taught him how to lift the horn but nothing on breathing, which comes naturally.

segments.title: Where he was born and raised
segments.summary: Born in the city; recalls early addresses before the tape runs out.

segments.chapter: Buddy Petit, Kid Thomas and working life
segments.title: Out-of-town dances with Buddy Petit and Kid Thomas on a 60-40 split
segments.summary: Reel 2. He worked with Kid Thomas about a year and Buddy Petit for a good while, playing Mississippi dances where the band got 40 percent.

segments.chapter: Buddy Petit, Kid Thomas and working life
segments.title: Buddy Petit's style, band and drummer Sammy Penn
segments.summary: Buddy played a six-piece band, soft, not a high-note man, and harmonized under Burbank's lead; Penn and George Washington played drums.

segments.chapter: Buddy Petit, Kid Thomas and working life
segments.title: Playing with many bands at once while keeping a day job
segments.summary: He might work with four bands in a week and kept a day job as stock cutter in a shoe factory.

segments.chapter: Buddy Petit, Kid Thomas and working life
segments.title: Whether music pays; wages and jukeboxes
segments.summary: Music is worth it to him; pay was about a dollar an hour, and jukeboxes later cut into the work.

segments.chapter: Buddy Petit, Kid Thomas and working life
segments.title: Danny Barker's first job in Burbank's lakefront trio
segments.summary: Danny Barker played banjo in his three-piece group at the lake every night for about a year; he carried the melody.

segments.title: Small groups and the low-down tunks he avoided
segments.summary: Allen asks about tunks and trio work; Burbank never went into the rough places (text heavily garbled).

segments.title: Blues clarinetists and whether style changes between bands
segments.summary: Blues were not a specialty; bandleader set the style, and trumpeters sounded the same with Petit as with Thomas.

segments.title: Trumpeters McLeod, Leonard Parker, Dan Moody and Lee Collins
segments.summary: Trumpet players he worked with, comparing Moody to Lee Collins and noting Collins played second trumpet in the Elite band.

segments.title: Personnel of the Olympia band
segments.summary: Tries to recall the Olympia band's trombonist, bass player Thomas Colton and banjoist; the ASR is garbled.

segments.title: Nicknames like King and Kid, and playing in funerals as the clarinet wizard
segments.summary: Few clarinetists took titles; he recalls a parade with two clarinets in different keys.

segments.title: Two clarinets in one band; Piku and Neely Barnes
segments.summary: With two clarinets they made separate variations; Piku wrote him a second part to High Society.

segments.title: Wooden Joe and how Bill Russell came to record him
segments.summary: He played with Wooden Joe, and Bill Russell's idea led to Burbank's recording.

segments.title: First clarinet, lessons, marriage and children
segments.summary: Got his clarinet at about 17 around 1919; Tio could not teach him; he married in 1923 and moved.

segments.title: Nephews who play music
segments.summary: Lists nephews on bass, drums, banjo and trombone, one playing rock and roll.

segments.title: Favorite bands, reading music and tempo differences
segments.summary: He enjoyed all the bands; none used orchestrations; Bushall reminded him of Buddy; bands differ mainly in tempo.

segments.title: First Mardi Gras playing alone in the street
segments.summary: Reel 3. Masked with his sister's factory girls, he blew clarinet all day.

segments.title: Eureka Brass Band around 1944-45
segments.summary: He played B-flat clarinet with Eureka for about a year, ignoring E-flat parts.

segments.title: McConnier, Happy Landings and pianist Joe Parker
segments.summary: Played carnival jobs and Happy Landings with pianist Joe Parker.

segments.title: Ernest Cagnolatti, Paul Barbarin and Joe Longagne
segments.summary: He worked with trumpeters Cagnolatti and Barbarin in the 30s and Longagne, who led a brass band and played Dixieland.

segments.title: Tempo, drummers, double time and piano versus banjo
segments.summary: Old drummers kept good time and doubled up with soloists; he names present-day drummers like Giles.

segments.title: First band with Johnny Dave and his stint with Kid Ory in California
segments.summary: His first band was a 1920s group with Johnny Dave; Ory sent for him and he played three months in California with Don Ewell on piano.

segments.title: His records and their reception
segments.summary: Sales and reviews of his records, including a New York Times critic.

segments.title: Bob Lyons and Perez, and playing loud
segments.summary: A few jobs with Lyons, a Saturday job with Perez, and whether he was louder than other clarinetists.

segments.title: Creole French at home, a lesson teacher and a home recording
segments.summary: His mother spoke French; he sings Creole songs; he had a few lessons and a home recording with Giles.

segments.title: The tunes he wrote, including Lucky Me
segments.summary: He has written two Dixieland tunes, copyrighted Lucky Me, and sings it.

segments.title: Decatur Street joints and horse-race jobs with Octave Crosby
segments.summary: Decatur Street had four-piece bands nightly; at the racetrack the band played between races for Crosby.

segments.title: Punch Miller and Percy Humphrey
segments.summary: Played with Punch only in an advertisement; with Percy Humphrey many spot jobs before the 1949 recordings.

segments.title: Louis Dumaine, Chris Kelly and Kid Thomas then and now
segments.summary: Never played with Dumaine, one job with Chris Kelly; Thomas's band hasn't changed.

segments.title: Closing
segments.summary: Allen ends the interview.
